drip.author: onionsgobrown
drip.title: Apple crisp is better than apple pie, and pie mostly gets credit for how much work the crust was
drip.body:
It's apple season, so here we go. Pie is a two-hour project where half your energy goes into a crust that's either soggy on the bottom or so good nobody notices the apples. Crisp is twenty minutes of work, the topping is basically a crumbly oat cookie, and every spoonful gets the crunchy part and the soft part together.

I'm not saying pie is bad. I'm saying if you served both blind to a table of people who didn't know which one took two hours, crisp wins more often than pie people want to believe. We love pie partly because we suffered for it.

comments.author: SousVideSuspect
comments.body: What you're describing is a texture-ratio problem, and you're right about it. A slice of pie is mostly soft filling, with browned crust only on the edges and bottom. A crisp puts browned topping on every single spoonful. More surface, more browning, more crunch per bite. Pie loses on geometry.

replies.author: onionsgobrown
replies.body: "Pie loses on geometry" is coming with me to Thanksgiving dinner.

comments.author: marinara_line
comments.body: My nonna made crostata, which is a pie that got tired of pretending, so I'm biased toward crust. But a proper all-butter crust is a completely different food from the pale soggy thing you're describing. You're comparing a great crisp to a bad pie.

replies.author: onionsgobrown
replies.body: Fair, but most pies in the wild ARE the bad pie. I'm comparing what people actually bake on a Sunday, not what's sitting in a bakery window.

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: Pie is the single and crisp is the deep cut. Everyone orders the pie because it's the famous one. Crisp is what the people in the kitchen eat standing over the pan after the guests leave.

comments.author: bagelfaction
comments.body: Pas d'accord. Pie travels. You carry a pie to a party in your two hands. A crisp goes in a dish you will never see again. The crust is a container, and containers matter.

drip.author: SousVideSuspect
drip.title: Slow cookers make most dinners worse, and we keep using them for the convenience, not the food
drip.body:
Slow cooker season is starting and I'm bracing myself. I know they're handy. Dump it in at 8, dinner at 6. But almost everything that comes out of one is a soft, faded, slightly watery version of what it could have been. Nothing browns in there. Nothing reduces. The lid traps every drop, so the sauce ends up thinner than it went in.

Brown the meat first, braise it low in the oven with the lid cracked, and you get the same set-and-forget with an actual sauce. The slow cooker isn't a cooking method, it's a scheduling method. Which is fine. Just be honest about which one you bought.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Kitchen realist here, and I'm half disagreeing. A scheduling method is exactly what a lot of people need on a Tuesday in October. A slightly faded chili that's ready when you walk in beats a perfect braise you never made because you got home at seven. The best dinner is the one that exists.

replies.author: SousVideSuspect
replies.body: "The best dinner is the one that exists" is annoyingly hard to argue with. Revised position: use the slow cooker, but brown the meat the night before. Five minutes, huge difference.

comments.author: vinyl_endgame
comments.body: This is the streaming argument wearing an apron. Convenience wins and quality quietly slips out the back door. That said, my mother's Sunday pot roast came out of a slow cooker for my entire childhood, and I would fight anyone who called it faded.

comments.author: protein_pancake
comments.body: Routine lover checking in: mine makes shredded chicken every Sunday and I will not be taking notes. It doesn't need a sauce. It needs to be protein in containers by Monday. For that job it's perfect.

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: Not a cook, but "it's a scheduling method, not a cooking method" works as a review of half the gadgets I own.

drip.author: b_side_believer
drip.title: Lyrics are the least important part of most great songs
drip.body:
Most people couldn't write out the words to half the songs they love. They've been singing the wrong ones for twenty years and the song still wrecks them every time. That isn't a failure of listening, it's the proof. The melody, the voice, the moment the drums come in, that's what's doing the work. The words are mostly there to give the singer something to shape.

I'm not saying lyrics don't matter. A great line is a great line. But if you swapped the words of your favourite song for a decent grocery list, sung exactly the same way, I think it would still get you more often than you'd like to admit.

comments.author: vinyl_endgame
comments.body: Hard no from the romantic corner. Plenty of songs are carried by the tune, sure. But the ones people still play fifty years later almost always have one line that lands like a letter addressed to you personally. The melody gets you into the room. The words are why you stay.

replies.author: b_side_believer
replies.body: "a letter addressed to you" is lovely, but notice you're describing one line. I'm talking about the other forty. the grocery list stands.

comments.author: reversecowbell
comments.body: Former band guy: we wrote our lyrics last, in the van, on the back of a setlist, about twenty minutes before recording. In all the years since, nobody has ever mentioned them. People mention the bass line. I rest my case, sadly.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Kitchen version of this: people swear they love a dish for the fancy ingredient, and it's really the salt and the browning. The lyrics are the saffron. Nice to have. Not why anyone went back for seconds.

comments.author: bagelfaction
comments.body: D'accord, and I have proof. Half of Montréal grew up singing along to English radio without understanding a word, and we loved those songs exactly as much. Maybe more. Our made-up words were better.

drip.author: vinyl_endgame
drip.title: Playing your favourite album at a dinner party is how you ruin it for yourself
drip.body:
Dinners are moving back indoors, so let me say it. When you put on a record you truly love while people eat and talk over it, you spend the whole night listening to your favourite song get ignored. Somebody laughs through the bridge. Somebody asks you to turn it down right before the best part.

Background music should be music you like but don't love. Save the records that matter for when someone actually wants to sit down and listen. You wouldn't read your favourite poem aloud while everyone's passing the potatoes.

comments.author: b_side_believer
comments.body: Agreed so hard it hurts. I put on a deep-cut record at a dinner once and a guest asked if it was the radio. I have not recovered.

comments.author: SousVideSuspect
comments.body: Pushback from the host's side: the food is the thing I love that night, and I'm fine with people talking over it. Everything at a dinner party is ambient. The music, the candles, the braise. If it's good, it gets noticed a little, and that little is the point.

replies.author: vinyl_endgame
replies.body: Nobody talks over your braise while it's actually in their mouth. The record never gets that courtesy.

comments.author: bagelfaction
comments.body: Unpopular opinion inside the unpopular opinion: the best dinner party soundtrack is a hockey game on mute in the next room. Everybody checks the score, nobody's favourite album gets hurt.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Hard agree, and it goes for food too. Never cook the dish you're proudest of for a big crowd. Make the reliable one. Save the forty-seven-minute onions for two people who'll actually notice.

drip.author: bagelfaction
drip.title: Late September is the best time to sit on a terrasse, and peak summer patio season is overrated
drip.body:
Everyone fights for a patio table in the middle of summer. You sweat into your chair, the sun's in your eyes, the wasps are in your drink, and the line to sit down is forty minutes.

Now? A sweater, a bowl of soup or a pint, the light going gold at six, and half the tables empty because everyone decided patio season ended with the long weekend. The heaters are coming out. The servers are relaxed. This is the good part and nobody shows up for it.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Mostly agree, one realism note: the wasps get pushier this time of year, not less. Once their nests stop raising young they go hunting for sugar. Your pint is in more danger this week than it was all summer.

replies.author: bagelfaction
replies.body: Okay, the wasps have tenure. But it's twelve degrees cooler, and they're slow in the cold. I can take them.

comments.author: vinyl_endgame
comments.body: The sound is better too. A summer patio is a wall of noise. In September you can hear the person across from you, and whatever's playing inside drifts out through the open door.

comments.author: SousVideSuspect
comments.body: Disagree on food grounds. Summer patio food is built for patios: cold beer, salads, things off the grill. September patio food is a bowl of soup going lukewarm in eleven minutes because the wind picked up. Thermodynamics is not on your side.

replies.author: bagelfaction
replies.body: That's what the heaters are for. Also, you eat soup fast. That's just manners.

comments.author: maplebound
comments.body: Ottawa agrees with you. A late-September patio is a farewell tour, and you go to the farewell tour even when it's a bit chilly, because the next show isn't until May.

late_comments.author: bagelfaction
late_comments.body: Found this thread late, and I have to report: walked up the mountain last weekend with one album on, in order, no shuffle. The handoff between two songs landed right as I reached the lookout. That doesn't happen on shuffle. Annoyed you were right.

late_comments.author: vinyl_endgame
late_comments.body: This thread talked me out of prepping five identical lunches this week. One pot of soup, one tray of roasted vegetables, mixed differently every day. Still a little samey. Still better than the bricks.
